DEPARTMENT 732 LAW AND MOTION RULINGS


Case Number: 21STCV39315    Hearing Date: July 29, 2026    Dept: 732

Grace Cherry v. Velur Enterprises, Inc., et al.. 

 

Wednesday, July 29, 2026 

 

 

 

CASE NUMBER: 21STCV39315 

 

OPPOSED 

___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Defendants Velur Enterprises, Inc. Velur Properties, LLC, Marylou Matienzo, and Dennis Pilien’s Motion for Terminating Sanctions. 

___________________________________________________________________ 

Facts: This is an action for fraud and rescission of contract. The Complaint alleges as follows. Plaintiff Grace Cherry (Plaintiff) was induced to purchase several real properties from Defendants Velur Enterprises, Inc. and Velur Properties, LLC (Velur) based on representations made by Velur’s agents, Defendants Marylou Matienzo and Dennis Pilien. (Complaint ¶¶¿12–13.) These representations, concerning adjacent property owners on development taking place in the area, were false. (Complaint ¶¶ 12–15.) Plaintiff relied on these representations in purchasing the properties, and would not have done so otherwise. (Complaint ¶ 16.) 

Procedural History: Plaintiff filed the Complaint on October 25, 2021, alleging seven causes of action: 

  1. Fraud 

  1. Rescission of Contract 

  1. Breach of Fiduciary Duty 

  1. Professional Negligence 

  1. Breach of Broker’s Duties 

  1. False Advertising 

  1. Business & Professions Code § 17200 

On March 22, 2022, this court granted Defendants’ unopposed demurrer to the Complaint without leave to amend. An order of dismissal was entered on April 15, 2022. 

On September 8, 2022, this court granted Plaintiff’s motion for relief from dismissal. 

Plaintiff filed a first amended complaint on October 10, 2022, alleging eight causes of action: 

  1. Fraud 

  1. Negligent Misrepresentation 

  1. Rescission of Contract 

  1. Breach of Fiduciary Duty 

  1. Professional Negligence 

  1. Breach of Broker’s Duties 

  1. False Advertising 

  1. Business & Professions Code § 17200 

This court on February 1, 2023, sustained Defendants’ demurrer to the FAC as to the third and fourth causes of action, without leave to amend, and granted the motion to strike as to the second cause of action for negligent misrepresentation. The court also directed Plaintiff to add several necessary parties. 

Plaintiff filed a Second Amended Complaint on March 27, 2023, alleging five causes of action: 

  1. Fraud 

  1. Professional Negligence 

  1. Breach of Statutory Brokers Duties 

  1. False Advertising 

  1. Business & Professions Code § 17200 

This court on April 13, 2023, granted in part Defendants’ motion to dismiss as to the prayer for rescission in the SAC. 

Defendants Velur Enterprises, Inc. Velur Properties, LLC, Marylou Matienzo, and Dennis Pilien filed the present motion for terminating sanctions on June 12, 2026. 

Plaintiff filed an opposition on July 17, 2026. 

Defendants filed a reply on July 22, 2026. 

Analysis: 

 

  1. MOTION FOR TERMINATING SANCTIONS 

The court may impose terminating sanctions, including an order striking pleadings, an order dismissing an action, or an order rendering judgment by default against a party, for conduct that is a misuse of the discovery process. (Code Civ. Proc., § 2023.030.) This conduct includes “[f]ailing to respond or to submit to an authorized method of discovery,” and “[d]isobeying a court order to provide discovery.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 2023.010.)  

Ultimate discovery sanctions are justified where there is a willful discovery order violation, a history of abuse, and evidence showing that less severe sanctions would not produce compliance with discovery rules.  (Van Sickle v. Gilbert (2011) 196 Cal.App.4th 1495, 1516.)  Dismissal is a drastic measure, and terminating sanctions should only be ordered when there has been previous noncompliance with a rule or order and it appears a less severe sanction would not be effective.  (Link v. Cater (1998) 60 Cal.App.4th 1315, 1326.)  “[A] penalty as severe as dismissal or default is not authorized where noncompliance with discovery is caused by an inability to comply rather than willfulness or bad faith.”  (Brown v. Sup. Ct. (1986) 180 Cal.App.3d 701, 707.) 

Defendants Velur Enterprises, Inc. Velur Properties, LLC, Marylou Matienzo, and Dennis Pilien (“Defendants”) move for terminating sanctions against Plaintiff grace Cherry, dismissal of her complaint for failure to prosecute, and for judgment on the pleadings, for the same single reason. On February 1, 2023, this court sustained Defendants’ demurrer to Plaintiff’s First Amended Complaint (“FAC”) in part upon the grounds of Plaintiff’s failure to join parties necessary for the adjudication of Plaintiff’s claim for rescission, including Odilon Aquino, Danilo S. Peralta, and Marinette C. Peterson,. (See 2/1/2023 Order.) Moreover, although Equity Trust was directed to be joined, and later was joined, Plaintiff dismissed that entity on January 6, 2026. Despite the ensuing years, the upcoming September 29, 2026 trial date, and the looming five-year trial deadline of Code of Civil Procedure § 583.310, Plaintiff has failed to serve these parties. (Ma Decl. ¶¶¿2–10.) Defendants thus argue that terminating sanctions are warranted for failure to abide by the court’s orders, for failure to diligently prosecute this matter under Code of Civil Procedure § 583.410, and for failure to state a cause of action based on the omission of indispensable parties.  

Plaintiff in opposition argues that no service is necessary upon the identified parties, as they were only made indispensable by Plaintiff’s cause of action and prayer for restitution, the first of which was dismissed from the FAC by the same court order that directed the addition of the necessary parties on February 1, 2023, and the latter of which was dismissed from the SAC by the order of April 13, 2023. ( Opposition at pp. 7–9; see 4/13/2023 Order.) Plaintiff argues that terminating sanctions are not warranted because Defendants do not present a pattern of willful misconduct such that terminating sanctions are warranted over lesser sanctions. (Opposition at pp. 9–11.) Plaintiff argues that dismissal for delay in prosecution is not appropriate because she has diligently appeared in this case and trial is fast approaching. (Opposition at pp. 11–13.) Plaintiff finally argues that no motion for judgment on the pleadings is warranted because no claim or prayer for relief is now pleaded that requires the joinder of the parties identified. (Opposition at pp. 13–14.) 

Defendants in reply argue that Plaintiff’s opposition was filed one day late and never served. (Young Decl. ¶ 4.)  

Terminating sanctions and judgment on the pleadings are not warranted.  This is because an order of sanctions for failing to obey a court order will generally not lie when the order is invalid or inoperative. (See People v. Sorden (2021) 65 Cal.App.5th 582, 593 [contempt sanctions require “a valid order”].) This court on February 1, 2023, directed Plaintiff to join certain parties on the grounds that they were indispensable to any to adjudication of Plaintiff’s claim and prayer for rescission.  This is because “[i]n an action for rescission of a contract, all parties to the contract are indispensable to the action.” (Holder v. Home Sav. & Loan Ass'n of Los Angeles (1968) 267 Cal.App.2d 91, 107.)  

But as Plaintiff notes in opposition, any such order to join these parties that was not obviated by the February 1, 2023 dismissal of the rescission cause of action from the FAC was mooted by the April 13, 2023 order directing the dismissal of Plaintiff’s prayer for rescission from the SAC. As the court stated in its latter ruling, “[t]he addition of the new parties was required because of Plaintiff's request for a specific form of relief: rescission of the contracts to which these other people were parties,” and “[t]he failure to add these necessary parties forecloses only Plaintiffs prayer for rescission; it does not prevent Plaintiff from seeking damages from injuries suffered particularly by her.” (4/13/2023 Ruling.) There being no operative prayer for rescission of the contract, there is no present basis to compel the joinder and service of the parties that Defendants identify, and thus no basis to sanction Plaintiff for failing to abide by a moot order. Defendants in reply offer no challenge to the reasoning of Plaintiff on this point.  

But between the entry of that order on February 1, 2023, and the filing of the present motion on June 12, 2026, more than three years have elapsed. In that span, the court has many times scheduled orders to show cause regarding the failure to serve or take the default of the parties, whom Plaintiff, regardless of the efficacy of the February 1, 2023 order, has in fact joined as Doe defendants. (See 3/27/2025 Order; 8/20/2025 Order; 10/24/2025 Order; 1/30/2026 Order; 3/2/2026 Order; 4/3/2026 Order; 6/9/2026 Order.) Plaintiff’s failure to dismiss, serve, or take the default of these defendants has led to the delay of trial in this action. (See 3/27/2025 Order [vacating trial date].) The court in its order of January 30, 2026, stated that the case was “not at issue” because “[n]ot all parties have been served.” (1/30/2026 Order.) Plaintiff in this time has not raised any argument concerning the necessity of serving, defaulting, or dismissing these parties, but has through February 2026 represented that she sought to serve them without success, most recently by publication (See 2/25/2026 Application for Publication), An order authorizing such service was made (See 2/27/2026 Order), but no such service has evidently been accomplished. It appears that Plaintiff in this time made no argument concerning the mootness of the February 1, 2023 order, until filing the opposition to the present motion on July 17, 2026.  

The above proceedings naturally raise a question of delay in prosecution of this action under Code of Civil Procedure § 583.410. Under that statute, “The court may in its discretion dismiss an action for delay in prosecution pursuant to this article on its own motion or on motion of the defendant if to do so appears to the court appropriate under the circumstances of the case.” (Code Civ. Proc. § 583.410,, subd. (a).) Dismissal may be granted upon the following conditions: 

(1) Service is not made within two years after the action is commenced against the defendant. 

 

(2) The action is not brought to trial within the following times: 

(A) Three years after the action is commenced against the defendant unless otherwise prescribed by rule under subparagraph (B). 

(B) Two years after the action is commenced against the defendant if the Judicial Council by rule adopted pursuant to Section 583.410 so prescribes for the court because of the condition of the court calendar or for other reasons affecting the conduct of litigation or the administration of justice.  

(Code Civ. Proc. § 583.420, subd. (a)(2).) The California Rules of Court (“CRC”) prescribe consideration of the following non-exclusive factors in considering dismissal under the above statute:  

In ruling on the motion, the court must consider all matters relevant to a proper determination of the motion, including: 

(1) The court's file in the case and the declarations and supporting data submitted by the parties and, where applicable, the availability of the moving party and other essential parties for service of process; 

(2) The diligence in seeking to effect service of process; 

(3) The extent to which the parties engaged in any settlement negotiations or discussions; 

(4) The diligence of the parties in pursuing discovery or other pretrial proceedings, including any extraordinary relief sought by either party; 

(5) The nature and complexity of the case; 

(6) The law applicable to the case, including the pendency of other litigation under a common set of facts or determinative of the legal or factual issues in the case; 

(7) The nature of any extensions of time or other delay attributable to either party; 

(8) The condition of the court's calendar and the availability of an earlier trial date if the matter was ready for trial; 

(9) Whether the interests of justice are best served by dismissal or trial of the case; and 

(10) Any other fact or circumstance relevant to a fair determination of the issue. 

The court must be guided by the policies set forth in Code of Civil Procedure section 583.130.1 

(CRC Rule 3.1342, subd. (e).) 

It appears from the above account of the facts, in relation to the above factors,  that dismissal may properly be entered as to Plaintiff’s claims against those parties ordered to be joined on February 1, 2023, i.e. Eric Gene Goduco, Ma Peciosa Goduco, Odilon Aquino, Marinette C. Peterson, and Danilo S. Peralta. These parties were added as defendants to this action based on their essential connection to the rescission cause of action and prayer for relief, which have long been dismissed. Plaintiff in that time has failed to serve Odilon Aquino, Danilo S. Peralta, and Marinette C. Peterson, has already dismissed Equity Trust, and has failed to take the default of the remainder. The sole claim for which these parties were ordered joined has been dismissed, Plaintiff has failed to serve all parties for whom adjudication of that claim would be necessary, and Plaintiff has no evident desire to prosecute any claim against these parties. Thus dismissal of Plaintiff’s claims in relation to them appears to be within the court’s discretion. 

But the moving and opposing papers here do not present adequate basis to conclude whether dismissal for delay in prosecution may be entered as to Plaintiff’s claims against moving Defendants. Defendants in their motion articulate only Plaintiff’s failure to diligently serve these other parties, (Motion at pp. 7–8), and in reply offer only conclusory invocations of prejudice arising from the delay. (Reply at pp. 5–6.) Plaintiff in opposition argues only that the delay is excusable, and that she has diligently participated in this action, largely by reference to the filing of amended pleadings, opposition to Defendant’s challenges thereto, and appearance at status conferences. (Opposition at pp. 11–13.) Trial is set for September of this year, but the parties’ materials do not permit a conclusion as to whether it may justly be held in light of the substantial delay that precedes it. The record is thus presently inadequate to determine whether discretionary dismissal is appropriate as to Plaintiff’s claims against the moving Defendants under Code of Civil Procedure § 583.410.  

Accordingly, the hearing on the present motion is CONTINUED to permit the parties to submit additional briefing concerning the appropriateness of dismissal in light of the factors described in CRC Rule 3.1342, subd. (e).

Case Number: 21STCV42024    Hearing Date: July 29, 2026    Dept: 732

Qasim Zaidi, et al. v. Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transit Authority., et al. 

 

Wednesday, July 29, 2026 

 

 

 

CASE NUMBER: 21STCV42024 

 

OPPOSED 

___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Defendants Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transit Authority and Walsh Shea Corridor Constructors’ Motion to Augment Expert Witness Designation 

 

Defendants Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transit Authority and Walsh Shea Corridor Constructors’ Motion to Compel Deposition of Plaintiffs’ Expert Jeff Hughes 

___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Facts: This is an inverse condemnation action. The Complaint alleges as follows. Plaintiffs Qasim Zaidi, Michael Whitted, Carolawyn Smith, Sharon Barnes, Bernyesha Hollins, Dana Pharr, and Cassandra Thompkins (Plaintiffs) own real property within one mile of railway construction performed by Defendants Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transit Authority and Wash Shea Corridor Constructors (Defendants) for the Crenshaw/LAX Transit Corridor. (Complaint ¶¶ 16–17.) The structures on Plaintiffs’ properties have been damaged and cracked by Defendants’ construction. (Complaint ¶¶ 18–21.)  

Procedural History: Plaintiffs filed the complaint on November 15, 2021, alleging three causes of action: 

  1. Negligence 

  1. Inverse Condemnation 

  1. Nuisance 

On April 20, 2022, this court granted Anthony O. Egbase and Aliyah J. Guidry of A.O.E. Law & Associates’ motion to be relieved as counsel for Plaintiff Dana Pharr. 

On December 7, 2022, this court granted Defendant LACMTA’s motions to compel responses to requests for production and interrogatories from Plaintiff Dana Pharr. 

On January 19, 2023, this court granted Defendant’s motion to inspect Dana Pharr’s property. 

On May 8, 2023, this court granted Defendant’s motion for terminating sanctions against Plaintiff Dana Pharr. 

On February 5, 2024, this court granted Plaintiff’s motion to continue trial. 

On March 14, 2025, this court granted in part Plaintiffs’ motion to augment expert witness designation, permitting the addition of their proposed expert Hughes on the condition that Plaintiffs pay for depositions made necessary by the augmentation. The court also granted in part Defendant’s motion to bifurcate trial, ruling that trial shall be divided into two phases, with the first phase addressed to the issue of liability on Plaintiffs’ inverse liability claim, tried to the court in the presence of a jury. The second phase of trial will address Plaintiffs’ compensation for the inverse condemnation claim, as well as Plaintiffs’ other claims, tried to the same jury. 

On August 20, 2025, the court denied Plaintiff’s motion to consolidate. 

Defendants filed the present motion to augment expert witness designation on June 24, 2026. Plaintiffs filed an opposition on July 8, 2026. Defendants filed a reply on July 22, 2026. 

Defendants filed the present motion to compel deposition testimony of Jeff Hughes on July 7, 2026. Plaintiffs filed an untimely opposition on July 22, 2026. Defendants filed a reply and notice of non-opposition on July 22, 2026. 

Analysis 

 

  1. MOTION TO AMEND EXPERT DESIGNATION 

(a) On motion of any party who has engaged in a timely exchange of expert witness information, the court may grant leave to do either or both of the following: 

 

(1) Augment that party's expert witness list and declaration by adding the name and address of any expert witness whom that party has subsequently retained. 

 

(2) Amend that party's expert witness declaration with respect to the general substance of the testimony that an expert previously designated is expected to give. 

 

(b) A motion under subdivision (a) shall be made at a sufficient time in advance of the time limit for the completion of discovery under Chapter 8 (commencing with Section 2024.010) to permit the deposition of any expert to whom the motion relates to be taken within that time limit. Under exceptional circumstances, the court may permit the motion to be made at a later time. 

 

(c) The motion shall be accompanied by a meet and confer declaration under Section 2016.040. 

 

(Code Civ. Proc.  2034.610.)  

The court shall grant leave to augment or amend an expert witness list or declaration only if all of the following conditions are satisfied: 

(a) The court has taken into account the extent to which the opposing party has relied on the list of expert witnesses. 

(b) The court has determined that any party opposing the motion will not be prejudiced in maintaining that party's action or defense on the merits. 

(c) The court has determined either of the following: 

(1) The moving party would not in the exercise of reasonable diligence have determined to call that expert witness or have decided to offer the different or additional testimony of that expert witness. 

(2) The moving party failed to determine to call that expert witness, or to offer the different or additional testimony of that expert witness as a result of mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or excusable neglect, and the moving party has done both of the following: 

(A) Sought leave to augment or amend promptly after deciding to call the expert witness or to offer the different or additional testimony. 

(B) Promptly thereafter served a copy of the proposed expert witness information concerning the expert or the testimony described in Section 2034.260 on all other parties who have appeared in the action. 

(Code Civ. Proc., § 2034.620, subd. (a)–(c).) Leave to augment must be conditioned on the moving party making the expert promptly available for deposition. (Code Civ. Proc. § 2034.620, subd. (d).) 

Defendants Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transit Authority and Walsh Shea Corridor Constructors (“Defendants”) seek leave to augment their expert witness lists to replace two experts presently designated  — Thomas Gillgren (“Gillgren”) and Mike Villalba (‘Villalba”) — with new experts designated to testify to the same matters, Michael V. Saunders (‘Saunders”) and Pete D. Fowler (“Fowler”).  

Defendants argue that the replacements are necessary because Gillgren, originally designated to testify concerning appraisals, has indicated as of April 21, 2026, to Defendants’ counsel that he is undergoing major surgery requiring several months of recovery, and as of June 22, 2026, informed Defendants’ counsel that he would be medically retiring and unable to continue working on this matter. (Ebel Decl. ¶ 4.)  

As to Villalba, Defendants contend that on May 28, 2026, they were informed that he would no longer be working at the firm (Peter Fowler Construction Services, Inc., or “PFCS”) through which he was retained. (Ebel Decl. ¶ 5.) 

Defendants argue that Plaintiffs Qasim Zaidi, Michael Whitted, Carolawyn Smith, Sharon Barnes, Bernyesha Hollins, Dana Pharr, and Cassandra Thompkins (collectively “Plaintiffs”) will not be prejudiced by permitting these replacements, because Plaintiffs never deposed Villalba, meaning they will not need to depose his replacement (Ebel Decl. ¶ 8), and because, although Plaintiffs deposed Gillgren, Defendants shall make Saunders immediately available for deposition. (Motion at p. 7.) 

Plaintiffs in opposition argue that Defendants have produced insufficient evidence to show that Gillgren and Villalba are legally unavailable, as the motion includes only the secondhand testimony of Defendant’s counsel. (Opposition at pp. 7–12.) Plaintiffs argue that they have substantially relied on Defendant’s designations in preparing their case for trial and preparing their motions in limine. (Ibid.)  

Plaintiffs’ arguments are not persuasive as to Defendants’ proposed replacement of Gillgren with Saunders. Defendants’ counsel declares, “On June 22, 2026, counsel spoke with Gillgren, who confirmed that he is medically retiring and will be unable to continue working on this matter.” (Ebel Decl. ¶ 4.) Regardless of whether Defendants present evidence concerning the facts of Gillgren’s underlying illnesses, the testimony of counsel as to Gillgren’s decision not to proceed with this matter is testimony concerning Gillgren’s conduct that is admissible regardless of whether the underlying reasons are taken as true. (See Evid. Code § 1200.) This information was relayed on June 22, 2026, and the present motion was brought promptly thereafter.  Defendants have thus complied with Code of Civil Procedure § 2034.620, subd. (c)(2). 

Plaintiffs present reasonable arguments to the effect that they have relied on Gillgren’s designation as an appraisal expert, and that they have accordingly deposed him and formulated trial strategy around his estimates. (Opposition at p. 10.) However, the prejudice to be suffered by allowing the substitution of Saunders does not extend to Plaintiffs’ ability to maintain their action on the merits, but rather to the additional work and expense associated with Saunders’ deposition and incorporating his analysis into their strategy. (Code Civ. Proc. § 2034.620, subd. (b).) The prejudice to be suffered is thus not much more than that associated with the augmentation of Plaintiffs’ own expert witness list by this court’s order of March 14, 2025. Such prejudice does not furnish a basis to deny the present motion, particularly in light of the absence of fault associated with the necessity of Gillgren’s substitution.  

However, Plaintiffs are correct that Defendants have not shown the necessity of Fowler’s substitution for Villalba. The sole basis for seeking this substitution is the declaration of Defendants counsel, not that Villalba cannot or will not testify, but that on May 28, 2026, Defendants were informed that Villalba “would no longer be working at PFCS.” (Ebel Decl. ¶ 5.) Defendants do not elaborate on the difficulty of retaining Villalba in reply, but argue, without authority, that his departure from the firm through which he was retained is a legitimate basis for seeking substitution. (Reply at pp. 2–3.) Defendants do not explain why Villaba’s departure from PFCS renders him unable to testify, or why the prejudice to Defendants from procuring his testimony now that he has departed the firm justifies the prejudice to be suffered by Plaintiffs in accounting for a new expert. It is true enough that Plaintiffs do not describe great deal of prejudice resulting from Villalba’s substitution, as they never deposed him, and cite only to one motion in limine in which they moved to exclude the testimony of another expert on the grounds that he failed to take measurements and relied on Villalba’s estimates in forming his own opinions. (Opposition at pp. 7–8.) This is not a great deal of prejudice resulting from the proposed substitution. But Defendants do not present justification for this proposed substitution, and absent such explanation as to why Fowler’s addition to the expert list  is the result of mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or excusable neglect under Code of Civil Procedure § 2034.602, subd. (c)(2), the motion will not be granted to permit Fowler’s substitution for Villalba.  

Accordingly, the motion is GRANTED as to the substitution of Saunders for Gillgren, conditioned upon Defendants making Saunders promptly available for deposition. The motion is DENIED as to the proposed substitution of Fowler for Villalba. 

  1. MOTION TO COMPEL DEPOSITION 

A party may make a motion compelling a witness’s deposition “after service of a deposition notice” if that witness “fails to appear for examination, or to proceed with it.” (Code Civ. Proc. § 2025.450, subd. (a).) The motion must include a meet-and-confer declaration and show good cause for the discovery sought. (Code Civ. Proc. § 2025.450, subd. (b)(1), (2).) 

Defendants move to compel the continued deposition of Jeff Hughes, which was held in part on September 12, 2025, until it was terminated after four hours by Plaintiffs, on the contention that they were directed, per this court’s order of March 14, 2025, to pay for only four hours of each deposition occasioned by Hughes’ introduction into this matter as an expert. (Ebel Decl. ¶¶ 7–8, Exh. F.) Defendants contend that the deposition was stopped before Hughes could testify concerning the cost estimate for Plaintiff Sharon Barnes. (Ebel Decl. ¶ 14.)  

Plaintiffs filed an opposition on July 22, 2026, a mere five court days before the hearing set on this motion, and thus untimely under Code of Civil Procedure § 1005, subd. (b), and depriving Defendants of a meaningful chance to respond. The argument asserted in this opposition is that Defendants have not been diligent in seeking a subsequent deposition under  Code of Civil Procedure § 2025.610. Yet Defendants do not seek a subsequent deposition under that statute, but rather to compel deposition that was prematurely cut off under Code of Civil Procedure § 2025.450. Defendants present evidence that the deposition was stopped after four hours upon Plaintiffs’ representation that they would not pay for more. But per the court’s order of March 14, 2025, and the associated transcript of the hearing, Plaintiffs were directed to pay for the Hughes deposition without the four-hour limitation. (Se 3/14/2025; Ebel Decl. Exh. A at p. 29.) Defendants thus make a showing of good cause for the resumption of the deposition.  

The motion to compel the deposition of Jeff Hughes is GRANTED. Said deposition shall resume within 20 days of this order.    

  1. Sanctions 

“If a motion under subdivision (a) is granted, the court shall impose a monetary sanction under Chapter 7 (commencing with Section 2023.010) in favor of the party who noticed the deposition and against the deponent or the party with whom the deponent is affiliated, unless the court finds that the one subject to the sanction acted with substantial justification or that other circumstances make the imposition of the sanction unjust.” (Code Civ. Proc. § 2025.450, subd. (e).)  

Defendants seek $2465.00 in sanctions, representing nine hours of attorney work at $285.00 per hour. (Ebel Decl. ¶ 15.) No sanctions are awarded.

Case Number: 22STCV36611    Hearing Date: July 29, 2026    Dept: 732

John Doe v. Roe Youth Organization 1, et al. 

 

Wednesday, July 29, 2026 

 

 

 

CASE NUMBER: 22STCV36611 

 

OPPOSED 

___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Plaintiff John Doe’s Motion to Compel Deposition Answers of Defendant Roe Mentor ___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Facts: This is an action based on liability for child sexual abuse. The Third Amended Complaint (TAC) alleges as follows. Plaintiff John Doe was a minor of 13 years old in 1991 when he was sexually abused by Defendant Roe Mentor. (TAC ¶ 23.) Roe Mentor was an agent, advisor, counselor, and/or volunteer for Defendant Roe Youth Organization 2, which was supervised by Roe Youth Organization 1. (TAC ¶ 23.) Defendants maintained Roe Mentor in his position despite having actual or constructive knowledge of Roe Mentor’s dangerous propensities. (TAC ¶ 28.)  

Procedural History: Plaintiff filed the original Complaint on November 21, 2022. Plaintiff filed a First Amended Complaint on December 14, 2022, and a Second Amended Complaint on October 6, 2023. Plaintiff filed the TAC on January 4, 2024, alleging five causes of action: 

  1. Negligence 

  1. Negligent Supervision/Training/Hiring/Retention 

  1. Sexual Battery 

  1. Assault 

  1. Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress 

Plaintiff filed the present motion to compel deposition answers on January 23, 2026. 

Defendant filed an opposition on July 16, 2026. 

Plaintiff filed a reply on July 22, 206.  

Analysis 

 

  1. MOTION TO COMPEL DEPOSITION ANSWERS 

“If a deponent fails to answer any question or to produce any document, electronically stored information, or tangible thing under the deponent's control that is specified in the deposition notice or a deposition subpoena, the party seeking discovery may move the court for an order compelling that answer or production.”  (Code Civ. Proc. § 2025.480, subd. (a).).  

Plaintiff John Doe (“Plaintiff”) moves to compel deposition answers and responses to requests for production contained in a deposition notice from Defendant Roe Mentor, (“Defendant”), based on Defendant’s refusal to answer questions or produce documents based on the invocation of his privilege against self-incrimination. (Motion at pp. 5–8.)  

The deposition at issue took place on December 9, 2025, following service of objections by Defendant to requests for production based on the privilege against self-incrimination, and following notice from his counsel hat he was not going to answer any “substantive questions” based on the same privilege. (Gamble Decl. ¶¶ 6–9.) At the deposition, Defendant answered questions concerning his name, birth date, address, marital status, and whether he had ever lived in California. (Gamble Decl. Exh. E at pp. 11–12.) When questioned concerning when he had lived in California, Defendant’s counsel suggested that he invoke the privilege, which he did. (Gamble Decl. Exh. E at p. 13.) Plaintiff’s counsel stated that any criminal statute of limitations had lapsed and thus Defendant could not invoke the privilege. (Id. at p. 13.) Defendant’s counsel disagreed, and stated that Plaintiff’s counsel could continue to ask questions, but he would instruct Defendant not to answer “anything that appears to be substantive.” (Id. At p. 14.)  

In the present motion, Plaintiff argues that Defendant cannot invoke the privilege against self-incrimination because the criminal statute of limitations has run on the alleged sexual abuse that is the subject of the present action. Per Plaintiff, under Penal Code § 801.1,  for qualifying sex crimes against a minor that are alleged to have been committed after January 1, 2015, or for which the limitations period had not expired as of January 1, 2015, prosecution may be initiated “any time prior to the victim's 40th birthday.” (Penal Code § 801.1, subd. (a).)  Plaintiff argues that he turned 40 in November 2017, meaning that the potential for any criminal prosecution expired on that date. (Motion at p. 6.)  

The privilege against self-incrimination may be asserted in civil proceedings. (See Warford v. Medeiros (1984) 160 Cal.App.3d 1035, 1042.)  

“The privilege afforded not only extends to answers that would in themselves support a conviction under a federal criminal statute but likewise embraces those which would furnish a link in the chain of evidence needed to prosecute the claimant for a federal crime. [Citation.] But this protection must be confined to instances where the witness has reasonable cause to apprehend danger from a direct answer. [Citation.] The witness is not exonerated from answering merely because he declares that in so doing he would incriminate himself—his say-so does not of itself establish the hazard of incrimination. It is for the court to say whether his silence is justified, [citation], and to require him to answer if ‘it clearly appears to the court that he is mistaken.’ [Citation.] However, if the witness, upon interposing his claim, were required to prove the hazard in the sense in which a claim is usually required to be established in court, he would be compelled to surrender the very protection which the privilege is designed to guarantee. To sustain the privilege, it need only be evident from the implications of the question, in the setting in which it is asked, that a responsive answer to the question or an explanation of why it cannot be answered might be dangerous because injurious disclosure could result. The trial judge in appraising the claim ‘must be governed as much by his personal perception of the peculiarities of the case as by the facts actually in evidence.’  

(Id. at p. 1043, quoting Hoffman v. United States (1951) 341 U.S. 479, 486–487.)   

A witness “need not demonstrate a real “likelihood of prosecution” in order to invoke the privilege against self-incrimination; rather, when a witness can show any possibility of prosecution which is more than fanciful, he has demonstrated a reasonable fear of prosecution sufficient to meet constitutional muster.”  (Warford, supra, 160 Cal.App.3d at p. 1044.) The witness may not assert a blanket refusal to testify, and “[t]he privilege must be specifically claimed on a particular question and the matter submitted to the court for its determination as to the validity of the claim.” (Id. at p. 1045.) “The reason for the requirement that the person claiming the privilege must object with specificity to the information sought from him is that only where this is done is the trial court enabled to make the particularized inquiry required of it. “A party is not entitled to decide for himself whether he is protected by the fifth amendment privilege. Rather, this question is for the court to decide after conducting ‘a particularized inquiry, deciding, in connection with each specific area that the questioning party seeks to explore, whether or not the privilege is well-founded.” (Ibid.)  

Defendant in opposition argues that the statute of limitations has not necessarily run as to the alleged abuse that is the subject of the present lawsuit. Specifically, Defendant notes Penal Code § 803, subd. (f), which states that “a criminal complaint may be filed within one year of the date of a report to a California law enforcement agency by a person of any age alleging that the person, while under 18 years of age, was the victim of a crime” to which the limitations period of Penal Code § 801.1, subd. (a) applies, permitting prosecution to take place, provided that each of the following conditions is met: 

(A) The limitation period specified in Section 800, 801, or 801.1, whichever is later, has expired. 

(B) The crime involved substantial sexual conduct, as described in subdivision (b) of Section 1203.066, excluding masturbation that is not mutual. 

(C) There is independent evidence that corroborates the victim's allegation. If the victim was 21 years of age or older at the time of the report, the independent evidence shall clearly and convincingly corroborate the victim's allegation. 

(Penal Code § 803, subd. (f).) Defendant thus argues that, notwithstanding the expiration of the limitations period of Penal Code § 801.1 with Plaintiff’s 40th birthday, he may still be subject to prosecution within one year of any qualifying report to a California law enforcement agency, supported by clear and convincing independent corroborating evidence. (Opposition at pp. 3–4.)  

Defendant’s argument is persuasive to the effect that he cannot be prevented from invoking the privilege on the grounds that he does not reasonably fear prosecution. Plaintiff argues that the conduct alleged in the Third Amended Complaint (“TAC”) constitute felony offenses subject to the limitations period of Penal Code § 801.1, and in reply does not dispute that the matters alleged constitute substantial sexual conduct under Penal Code § 1203.066. Thus a qualifying report supported by sufficient independent corroborating evidence would be effective to permit a criminal prosecution, despite the fact that the limitations period of Penal Code § 801.1 has already run. 

Plaintiff in reply argues that Defendant cannot invoke Penal Code §¿803 because he cannot say that any such report has been filed, or that any such evidence exists. (Reply at pp. 4–5.) Plaintiff analogizes the present case to Blackburn v. Superior Court (1993) 21 Cal.App.4th 414, 426, another child molestation case, in which the defendant sought to invoke the privilege against self-incrimination after the statute of limitations for criminal prosecution had run. The defendant there argued that “even though the prescribed period of limitations ha[d] expired, he still may be subject to criminal prosecution” because “the six-year statute of limitations may have been tolled.” (Blackburn, supra, 21 Cal.App.4th at p. 426.) The appellate court rejected the argument based on tolling, as it was supported by no other evidence save “counsel’s belief” that the limitations period might have been tolled.  (Id. at p. 429.)   

Blackburn is distinguishable. Defendant’s argument related to the statute of limitations rests not on an unspecified tolling doctrine but on the provisions of Penal Code § 803, subd. (f). Per those provisions, the limitations period may be reopened on the crimes alleged in the complaint here if report is made supported by sufficient corroborating evidence. Although Plaintiff argues that no such report has been made, the possibility that such report may be made is “more than fanciful,” particularly given Plaintiff’s allegations in the present action.(Warford, supra, 160 Cal.App.3d at p. 1044.) So too is the possibility that any such report would be supported by the requisite evidence. Indeed, the very deposition testimony that Plaintiff seeks here may provide the corroborating evidence that is used to satisfy the requirements of Penal Code § 803. Thus, even if a prosecution under that statute is unlikely, it is possible. “The test is whether the statement might tend to incriminate, not whether it might tend to lead to an actual prosecution or, stated slightly differently, whether the statement could, not would, be used against the witness.” (People v. Seijas (2005) 36 Cal.4th 291, 305, italics in original.)  The privilege against self-incrimination thus cannot be discarded here on the argument that the limitations period has run.   

Plaintiff in reply argues  that even if the privilege may be invoked, it may not be invoked in a blanket fashion against all questioning. (Reply at pp. 6–7.) It is true that a witness “may not assert a blanket refusal to testify, and “[t]he privilege must be specifically claimed on a particular question and the matter submitted to the court for its determination as to the validity of the claim.” (Warford, supra, 160 Cal.App.3d at p. 1045.) But the circumstances here do not present a blanket refusal to testify. Defendant has agreed to sit for his deposition, and has answered questions concerning his identity. His counsel has stated that objections shall be raised to “substantive” questions as they are asked, but resolution of whether these objections are proper or improper awaits the asking of the questions.  

The deposition transcript presents only one question asked of Defendant against which he invoked the privilege before deposition was suspended: “Can you tell me when you lived in California?” (Gamble Decl. Exh. E at p. 13.) Defendant argues that questions concerning when he lived in California seek incriminating information, because Plaintiff alleges he was abused by Defendant while he lived with him in 1991 and 1992. (Opposition at pp. 5–6; Statman Decl. ¶ 3.) It reasonably appears that the question could furnish “a link in the chain of evidence needed to prosecute the claimant for a  … crime.” (Warford, supra, 160 Cal.App.3d at p. 1043.)  

Likewise, Defendant’s objections to the requests for production of documents are also largely well-taken. These requests ask Defendant to produce documents concerning notice that he had committed or been accused of sexual abuse, communications relating to Plaintiff or the organizations he is alleged to have been affiliated with in the course of the alleged abuse of Plaintiff, (Gamble Decl. Exh. A.) Defendant’s possession of the records sought could once again form a link in the chain of evidence used to prosecute him.  

The sole exceptions appear to be Requests No. 9–11, which ask only for the production of documents identified in responses to interrogatories and requests for admissions. (Ibid.) As to these, Defendant makes no showing of any tendency to incriminate, and the court lacks reference to the responses to interrogatories or admissions at issue, and thus any basis to validate the exercise of the privilege as to these requests. 

Accordingly, the motion to compel deposition answers is GRANTED as to Requests for Production No. 9–11. As to the deposition questions themselves, the motion is DENIED, as Plaintiff has not identified any question that Defendant has wrongly refused to answer. No sanctions are awarded.

Case Number: 26STCV06410    Hearing Date: July 29, 2026    Dept: 732

 

 

Carey Booker v. Center of Toxicology and Environmental Health, Inc.., et al. 

 

Wednesday, July 29, 2026 

 

 

 

CASE NUMBER: 26STCV06410 

 

OPPOSED 

___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Defendants Montrose Environmental Group, Inc. and Center of Toxicology and Environmental Health, Inc.’s Demurrer to the First Amended Complaint ___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Facts: This is an action for employment discrimination. The First Amended Complaint (“FAC”) alleges as follows. Plaintiff Carey Booker (“Plaintiff”) was the only African-American employed by Defendants Montrose Environmental Group, Inc. and Center of Toxicology and Environmental Health, Inc. (“Defendants”) to work on a certain project in Valencia, California. (FAC ¶¶ 10–15.) After Plaintiff reported an incident in which another employee appeared intoxicated, project management confronted Plaintiff with false allegations from staff at the hotel where employees were housed that charged Plaintiff with intoxication, inappropriate touching, and purchasing alcohol for minors. (FAC ¶¶¿17–19.) Rather than perform an investigation or credit Plaintiff’s denials, Defendants terminated Plaintiff’s employment. (FAC ¶¶ 20–28.)  

Procedural History: Plaintiff filed the original Complaint on February 26, 2026, and filed the FAC on March 6, 2026, alleging five causes of action: 

  1. FEHA Race Discrimination 

  1. Lab. Code § 1102.5 Retaliation 

  1. Wrongful Termination 

  1. Defamation 

  1. Failure to Provide Rest Days 

Defendants filed the present demurrer on April 27, 2026. 

Plaintiff filed an opposition on July 16, 2026. 

Defendants filed a reply on July 22, 2026. 

Analysis 

  1. DEMURRER 

A demurrer should be sustained only where the defects appear on the face of the pleading or are judicially noticed. (Code Civ. Pro., §§ 430.30, et seq.) In particular, as is relevant here, a court should sustain a demurrer if a complaint does not allege facts that are legally sufficient to constitute a cause of action.¿(See id.¿§ 430.10, subd. (e).) As the Supreme Court held in Blank v. Kirwan (1985) Cal.3d 311: “We treat the demurrer as admitting all material facts properly pleaded, but not contentions, deductions or conclusions of fact or law. . . . Further, we give the complaint a reasonable interpretation, reading it as a whole and its parts in their context.”¿(Id. at p. 318; see also Hahn. v. Mirda (2007) 147 Cal.App.4th 740, 747 [“A demurrer tests the pleadings alone and not the evidence or other extrinsic matters. Therefore, it lies only where the defects appear on the face of the pleading or are judicially noticed. [Citation.]”)  

 

“In determining whether the complaint is sufficient as against the demurrer … if on consideration of all the facts stated it appears the plaintiff is entitled to any relief at the hands of the court against the defendants the complaint will be held good although the facts may not be clearly stated.”  (Gressley v. Williams (1961) 193 Cal.App.2d 636, 639.) 

 

“A demurrer for uncertainty is strictly construed, even where a complaint is in some respects uncertain, because ambiguities can be clarified under modern discovery procedures.” (Khoury v. Maly’s of Cal., Inc. (1993) 14 Cal.App.4th 612, 616.) Such demurrers “are disfavored, and are granted only if the pleading is so incomprehensible that a defendant cannot reasonably respond.” (Mahan v. Charles W. Chan Insurance Agency, Inc. (2017) 14 Cal.App.5th 841, 848.) 

 

A demurrer should not be sustained without leave to amend if the complaint, liberally construed, can state a cause of action under any theory or if there is a reasonable possibility the defect can be cured by amendment. (Schifando v. City of Los Angeles, supra, 31 Cal.4th at p. 1081.) The demurrer also may be sustained without leave to amend where the nature of the defects and previous unsuccessful attempts to plead render it probable plaintiff cannot state a cause of action. (Krawitz v. Rusch (1989) 209 Cal.App.3d 957, 967.) 

 

Defendants Montrose Environmental Group, Inc. and Center of Toxicology and Environmental Health, Inc. (“Defendants”) demurrer to the fourth cause of action for defamation contained in the First Amended Complaint (“FAC”) of Plaintiff Carey Booker (“Plaintiff”) on the grounds that the claim is time-barred. (Demurrer at pp. 3–4.)  

 

The time to bring an action for defamation is within one year of the defamatory publication. (Code Civ. Proc. § 340, subd. (c).) “As a general rule a cause of action for libel accrues when the defamatory matter is published.” (Schneider v. United Airlines, Inc. (1989) 208 Cal.App.3d 71, 76.)  

 

Here, the FAC alleges the defamatory matter to consist of “statements to [Defendants’] management and decision-makers asserting that Plaintiff engaged in improper and potentially unlawful conduct, including allegations that he attempted to purchase alcohol for an underage individual, behaved inappropriately toward hotel staff, or attempted to leave the hotel while intoxicated.” (FAC ¶¿56.) The FAC alleges that Plaintiff learned of these statements prior to his termination in August 2024, and that they formed Defendants’ asserted basis for his termination. (FAC ¶¶ 19, 24.) Thus under the one-year limitations period, any defamation claim based on these statements would have to be brought by August 2025. Because the Complaint here was not filed until February 2026, the defamation claim is time-barred as pleaded. 

 

Plaintiff in opposition argues that the facts pleaded do not foreclose republication of the defamatory matters within the limitations period, and the FAC contains a reference to republication. (Opposition at pp. 3–4.) But while the FAC contains an allegation that Plaintiff suffered harm as a result of “Defendants’ publication and republication of these false statements” (FAC ¶ 61), there is no allegation of publication or republication that post-dates Plaintiff’s August 2024 termination. Although Plaintiff argues that the cause of action may be tolled by delayed discovery (Opposition at p. 5), the facts establishing delayed discovery tolling must be pleaded with specificity. (See Fox v. Ethicon Endo-Surgery, Inc. (2005) 35 Cal.4th 797, 808.) Plaintiff alleges neither discovery-rule tolling nor facts justifying its application.  And while Plaintiff also argues that compelled self-republication may support a claim for defamation within the limitations period (Opposition at p. 5), again, no such theory is pleaded in the FAC. 

 

Accordingly, the demurrer is SUSTAINED as to the fourth cause of action, with leave to amend. Any amended pleading shall be filed within 20 days of this order.
